chapter_summary:
Now that we've explored the strategic horizon of release planning, it's time to zoom in on the tactical heart of Agile: Sprint Planning. For Scrum teams, Sprint Planning is a crucial event that kicks off every new sprint, setting the direction for the upcoming iteration. It's where the development team, guided by the Product Owner, collaboratively decides what work will be accomplished in the sprint and how that work will be done. This isn't just a meeting; it's a commitment ceremony, where the team makes a collective pledge to deliver a valuable, potentially shippable increment by the end of the sprint. Without effective Sprint Planning, a sprint can quickly lose focus, leading to wasted effort and missed opportunities for value delivery.

The Sprint Planning meeting typically has two main topics: "What will be done in this Sprint?" and "How will the chosen work get done?" The "What" part involves the Product Owner presenting the highest-priority items from the Product Backlog, explaining their business value and answering any questions the development team might have. The team then collaboratively selects a subset of these items that they believe they can realistically complete within the sprint, based on their capacity and historical velocity. This selection isn't a unilateral decision by the Product Owner; it's a negotiation and a commitment from the development team. A common mistake here is for the Product Owner to dictate the sprint scope or for the team to overcommit, leading to unfinished work and demoralization. The goal is a realistic and achievable commitment that delivers maximum value.

The "How" part of Sprint Planning is where the development team takes ownership. For each selected Product Backlog Item (typically a user story), the team discusses how they will turn it into a "Done" increment. This often involves breaking down the user story into smaller, more manageable tasks. For example, a user story like "As a customer, I want to reset my password so I can regain access to my account" might be broken down into tasks such as: "Create password reset API endpoint," "Design password reset UI," "Implement password reset form validation," "Write unit tests for API," "Integrate UI with API," and "Deploy to staging environment." This task breakdown helps the team understand the technical work involved, identify dependencies, and estimate the effort for each task. It also fosters a shared understanding of the work and promotes collaboration within the team.

A critical outcome of Sprint Planning is the **Sprint Goal**. This is a short, concise statement that defines the overarching objective for the sprint. It provides focus and flexibility. For instance, instead of just saying "Complete stories X, Y, Z," a Sprint Goal might be "Enable secure password reset functionality for all users." This goal provides a guiding star for the team. If during the sprint, a technical challenge arises that prevents completing a specific story exactly as planned, the team can still work towards the Sprint Goal by finding alternative solutions or adjusting scope, rather than rigidly adhering to individual story completion. The Sprint Goal also helps stakeholders understand the value being delivered in the sprint without getting bogged down in individual story details. It's a powerful tool for communication and alignment.

Capacity planning is an essential element of effective Sprint Planning. Before committing to work, the team needs to understand its available capacity for the upcoming sprint. This involves accounting for holidays, planned vacations, training, and other non-development activities. For example, if a team of five developers usually has 100 person-days of capacity in a two-week sprint, but one developer is on vacation for five days and another has a two-day training, their effective capacity is reduced. Ignoring capacity leads to overcommitment and missed sprint goals. Teams often use historical velocity as a guide, but they must adjust it based on current capacity. Another common mistake is neglecting to allocate a small percentage of capacity for unplanned work, bug fixes, or technical debt, which can derail a sprint if not accounted for. By focusing on a clear Sprint Goal, realistic capacity, and collaborative task breakdown, teams can significantly improve their chances of delivering a valuable increment every sprint.

screens.title: Iteration / Sprint Planning
screens.subtitle: Kick off every sprint with a clear goal, realistic commitments, and a shared plan for how work will get done.

narration.text: Sprint Planning is the tactical heart of Scrum where the team turns product direction into a short, focused plan. In this lesson you will learn why Sprint Planning is more than a meeting: it is a commitment ceremony that sets a Sprint Goal, selects backlog items the team can realistically deliver, and defines the technical steps to reach the goal. We will explore the two central questions asked in every Sprint Planning: what will be done this sprint, and how will that work be accomplished? You will see how task breakdown, capacity planning, and a concise Sprint Goal together prevent wasted effort, reduce uncertainty, and keep the team aligned with stakeholder value. Throughout, watch for common missteps such as the Product Owner dictating scope, teams overcommitting, or forgetting to account for reduced capacity. By the end of this chapter you will be able to lead or participate in Sprint Planning with techniques that produce a usable Sprint Backlog and a Sprint Goal that guides decisions during the sprint. Consider: how would a sharp Sprint Goal change the way your team decides which stories to keep or defer?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Sprint Planning pairs a realistic selection of backlog items with a shared plan and a clear Sprint Goal so a team can reliably deliver value each iteration.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you will build for effective Sprint Planning

narration.text: These objectives show what you will be able to do after this chapter. First, you will understand the purpose and structure of Sprint Planning so you can participate meaningfully and avoid common misunderstandings. Second, you will learn to craft a clear, achievable Sprint Goal that guides trade-offs during execution. Third, you will gain the ability to select and commit to Product Backlog Items based on capacity and historical velocity, preventing overcommitment. Finally, you will practice breaking down user stories into actionable tasks so the team has a shared technical plan and can estimate work. Each objective ties to a concrete classroom practice: drafting a Sprint Goal, negotiating scope with the Product Owner, calculating capacity for a sprint, and decomposing a story into tasks for front-end, back-end, testing, and deployment. These are practical skills: knowing the ceremony’s purpose is useful, but the measured ability to translate a backlog item into a sprint-ready plan is what helps teams deliver consistent value.

screens.title: What is Sprint Planning?
screens.subtitle: A time-boxed event to agree on what will be done and how to do it

narration.text: Sprint Planning is a time-boxed ceremony where the Scrum Team makes a shared commitment about the upcoming sprint. In practice this means the Product Owner presents high-priority Product Backlog Items, explains their business value, and answers clarifying questions. The Development Team then negotiates what subset of those items it can realistically finish, given historical velocity and current capacity. The purpose is to produce a Sprint Backlog and a Sprint Goal that together enable focused delivery. A clear example: the Product Owner asks for three customer-facing stories; the team evaluates them against available person-days and decides to take the highest-value two and one smaller technical fix, because that mix best fits their capacity. A common misconception is treating Sprint Planning as a task assignment meeting where the Product Owner tells the team what to do. That undermines team ownership and leads to missed commitments. The right practice is collaborative selection and negotiation. Key signals of a healthy planning session include clarifying questions, shared task breakdowns, and an explicit Sprint Goal. To check your understanding, ask: which single metric or conversation convinced the team to drop or include a story?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A jointly run, time-boxed planning event that produces a Sprint Backlog and a guiding Sprint Goal.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › What is Sprint Planning?
Definition

A collaborative commitment ceremony

Sprint Planning produces the Sprint Backlog and a Sprint Goal. It answers the two questions: what will be done, and how will it get done?

Example scenario
Team selects two customer stories and one small tech task to match capacity.
Misconception
Not a place for the Product Owner to unilaterally set scope; selection is collaborative.
Key Takeaway

Sprint Planning turns priority into a realistic plan and an aligned Sprint Goal that the team owns.

Quick checklist
  • Product Owner presents highest-priority items and value.
  • Team asks clarifying questions and inspects acceptance criteria.
  • Team selects items by capacity and velocity.
  • Team breaks stories into tasks and records estimates.
  • Team agrees on a single Sprint Goal.
Check your understanding
Reflection
What evidence did the team use to judge whether a set of items matched their capacity?

screens.title: The "What": Selecting Product Backlog Items
screens.subtitle: Negotiation and realistic selection based on value and capacity

narration.text: The "What" part of Sprint Planning focuses on selecting the Product Backlog Items the team will attempt to deliver. The Product Owner presents items in priority order and explains why they matter so the team can evaluate trade-offs. Selection is a negotiation: the Development Team assesses each item against capacity and historical velocity, then offers a realistic set of items it can commit to. A concrete example is helpful. If the team’s two-week velocity is about 25 story points and the top five backlog items sum to 40 points, the team must negotiate: which items deliver the most value within 25 points? A common error is allowing the Product Owner to dictate the sprint scope or for the team to accept optimistic estimates without discussing dependencies. Instead, teams should ask clarifying questions, reveal hidden complexity, and prioritize the most valuable subset. Keep a small buffer for unplanned urgent work. To validate selection, the team should be able to state why each chosen item contributes to the Sprint Goal and how it fits the available capacity. The "What": Selecting Product Backlog Items means choose backlog items by prioritised value and realistic capacity; negotiate scope rather than accepting dictation or overcommitment.. In practical terms, negotiation and realistic selection based on value and capacity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Selection principle
keyIdea.text: Choose backlog items by prioritised value and realistic capacity; negotiate scope rather than accepting dictation or overcommitment.

screens.title: The "How": Breaking Stories into Tasks
screens.subtitle: Decompose user stories into actionable tasks that reveal dependencies and effort

narration.text: The "How" part of Sprint Planning is where the Development Team takes ownership. For each selected Product Backlog Item, the team discusses how to turn it into a Done increment by breaking the story into smaller tasks. This task breakdown makes technical work visible, uncovers dependencies, and supports more accurate estimates. For example, a password reset story can be split into creating an A P I endpoint, designing the UI, implementing client-side validation, writing unit tests, integrating UI and A P I, and deploying to staging. Each task should have a clear owner and an effort estimate. A common misconception is that only detailed task lists guarantee success. In fact, over-detailing can add overhead; the aim is manageable tasks that enable flow and coordination. A good practice is to balance granularity so tasks are small enough to complete in a day or less, while avoiding micro-tasks that disrupt momentum. Before the sprint starts, ensure tasks reflect cross-functional work—front-end, back-end, QA, and deployment steps—and validate that together they map back to the acceptance criteria of the story. The "How": Breaking Stories into Tasks means break stories into cross-functional tasks small enough to finish quickly while keeping the team aligned on acceptance criteria.. In practical terms, decompose user stories into actionable tasks that reveal dependencies and effort. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Decomposition
keyIdea.text: Break stories into cross-functional tasks small enough to finish quickly while keeping the team aligned on acceptance criteria.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Breaking Stories into Tasks
Process

From story to tasks

Decompose each selected story into tasks that expose technical work, dependencies, owners, and effort estimates.

Example breakdown
User story: As a customer, I want to reset my password so I can regain access.

- Create password reset API endpoint (owner: backend) — 6h
- Design password reset UI (owner: frontend) — 4h
- Implement client-side form validation (owner: frontend) — 3h
- Write unit tests for API (owner: backend) — 4h
- Integrate UI with API (owner: full-stack) — 5h
- Deploy feature to staging (owner: devops) — 2h
Key Takeaway

Task breakdown clarifies work and supports reliable sprint commitments when tasks are sized sensibly and have owners.

Guidance
  • Keep tasks small enough to finish in a day or less.
  • Assign tentative owners and note dependencies.
  • Ensure tasks collectively satisfy the story acceptance criteria.
  • Avoid micromanaging; preserve team ownership and flow.
Check
Misconception
More granular tasks are not always better; they can increase overhead and reduce flexibility.

screens.title: Sprint Goal
screens.subtitle: A concise purpose that provides focus and flexibility

narration.text: The Sprint Goal is a short, single objective created during Sprint Planning that explains why the team is building the increment. It differs from a list of stories because the goal captures the value and intent, not just tasks completed. For example, rather than enumerating stories, a Sprint Goal might read: 'Enable customers to securely access and review their purchase history.' That goal allows the team to make trade-offs during the sprint while preserving value: if a specific story proves harder than expected, the team can find an alternative that still moves toward the goal. A common mistake is framing the goal as a checklist: 'Complete stories X, Y, Z.' That reduces flexibility and removes a guiding decision rule during uncertainty. A strong Sprint Goal helps stakeholders understand the sprint outcome without needing story-level detail and helps the team prioritize mid-sprint when unforeseen work arises. To apply this, practice converting a set of planned stories into one sentence that describes the customer benefit and the problem being solved. Sprint Goal means a concise objective that focuses the team and enables flexible trade-offs while preserving the sprint’s value.. In practical terms, a concise purpose that provides focus and flexibility. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Sprint Goal concept
keyIdea.text: A concise objective that focuses the team and enables flexible trade-offs while preserving the sprint’s value.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Sprint Goal
Definition & purpose

One guiding objective

The Sprint Goal explains why the increment matters. It keeps the team aligned and enables scope adjustments in service of value.

Good example

Bad example

screens.title: Capacity Planning & Velocity
screens.subtitle: How to size a sprint using availability and historical performance

narration.text: Capacity planning is the practical calculation that turns velocity into a usable commitment. Start with team-level historical velocity as a guide, then adjust it for the upcoming sprint by accounting for holidays, vacations, training, and other non-development activities. For example, if a five-person team normally records 100 person-days across a two-week sprint but two people have scheduled time off that reduces total days by 7, the effective capacity is lower. Teams commonly err by using raw historical velocity without adjusting for present availability, which leads to overcommitment. Another subtle mistake is forgetting to reserve some capacity for unplanned work and bug fixes. A good practice is to compute available person-days, convert to story points using your usual velocity-to-points mapping, and then select backlog items that fit within that adjusted budget. This process helps the team set realistic expectations and maintain a sustainable pace. To check your judgment, always ask: have we accounted for non-development commitments and left a buffer for unforeseen integration work? Capacity Planning & Velocity means adjust historical velocity for current availability and reserve buffer for unplanned work to avoid overcommitment.. In practical terms, how to size a sprint using availability and historical performance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Capacity principle
keyIdea.text: Adjust historical velocity for current availability and reserve buffer for unplanned work to avoid overcommitment.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Capacity Planning & Velocity
Comparison

Historical velocity vs. adjusted capacity

Use velocity as a guide. Adjust for current sprint availability and leave a buffer for unplanned work.

Historical velocity
Average points from past sprints
Adjusted capacity
Velocity reduced by planned absences
Practice
Convert available person-days to story points and select items to fit that budget.
Key Takeaway

Capacity must reflect the sprint’s actual availability, not just historical averages.

Scenario
Team usual velocity: 25 points. Planned absences reduce capacity by 20%. Practical selection should reflect closer to 20 points or less.
Check
Misconception
Treating velocity as an exact quota rather than a guide that must be adjusted for availability.

screens.title: Sprint Backlog and Commitment
screens.subtitle: From selected items to a plan of tasks the team owns

narration.text: The Sprint Backlog is the set of Product Backlog Items selected for the sprint plus the plan for delivering them. It is not just a static list but a dynamic artifact that includes tasks, owners, and estimates. The Development Team owns the Sprint Backlog and adapts it as work progresses. For example, after selecting three stories, the team decomposes each story into tasks, assigns owners, and tracks remaining work. If a task reveals a previously hidden dependency, the team updates the backlog and re-plans within the sprint to stay aligned with the Sprint Goal. A common pitfall is recording the backlog without task-level clarity; this leaves room for assumption and uneven work distribution. Another error is treating the Sprint Backlog as immutable. Instead, the team should update it daily to reflect discoveries while preserving the commitment to the Sprint Goal. At the end of planning, ensure every selected story maps to tasks and that the team can explain how the combined tasks will deliver a shippable increment. Sprint Backlog and Commitment means a team-owned plan of selected backlog items plus the tasks, owners, and estimates needed to deliver them.. In practical terms, from selected items to a plan of tasks the team owns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Sprint Backlog
keyIdea.text: A team-owned plan of selected backlog items plus the tasks, owners, and estimates needed to deliver them.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Sprint Backlog & Commitment
Definition

A living plan the team owns

The Sprint Backlog contains chosen items and the tasks needed to deliver them. The team updates it as new information appears.

What it contains
Selected stories, task breakdowns, owners, and remaining work estimates.
Good practice
Update backlog daily; keep tasks visible so the whole team can collaborate and help.
Key Takeaway

The Sprint Backlog is both a commitment and a tool for adaptation; own it and keep it current.

Quick example
Selected stories: Order history list, order detail page, API pagination. Tasks: API query, UI list, integration tests, styling, deploy to staging. Each task has an owner and estimate.
Check
Misconception
Treating the Sprint Backlog as immutable prevents necessary adaptations that preserve the Sprint Goal.

Next, use a hypothetical team velocity—say 25 points—and decide which backlog items fit. A recommended task list might include backend A P I development, query optimization, front-end list UI, order detail UI, integration of frontend with A P I, unit and integration tests, and staging deployment. For each task, assign an owner and a rough estimate in hours or points. Remember to note assumptions such as existing authentication. A common mistake learners make is listing tasks without tying them back to acceptance criteria. Ensure each task contributes to meeting the story’s acceptance criteria. Finally reflect: which task carries the greatest technical risk and how will you mitigate it during the sprint? Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Sprint Planning Simulation
Step-by-step
  1. Draft a Sprint Goal that states the customer benefit.
  2. Use velocity (e.g., 25 points) and adjust for availability.
  3. Select backlog items that fit the adjusted budget.
  4. Break one chosen story into 5–7 tasks with owners and estimates.

Example task list
User Story: As a registered customer, I want to view my past orders so I can track purchases.

- Backend API: /api/orders/{customerId} — 8h (owner: backend)
- DB query & optimization — 6h (owner: backend)
- Frontend: Order list component — 10h (owner: frontend)
- Frontend: Order detail view — 12h (owner: frontend)
- Integrate frontend with API — 7h (owner: full-stack)
- Unit & integration tests — 9h (owner: qa/backend)
- Deploy to staging — 4h (owner: devops)
Assumptions: authentication exists; UI follows design system. Reflection: which task is the riskiest and what mitigation will you plan?

screens.title: Pitfalls and the Scrum Master's Role
screens.subtitle: Avoid overcommitment, scope dictation, and neglected capacity

narration.text: Sprint Planning often derails because of a few recurring mistakes. First, overcommitment occurs when teams accept more work than their adjusted capacity allows. This happens when historical velocity is applied without considering current availability or when optimistic estimates are not challenged. Second, scope dictation by the Product Owner removes team ownership and leads to morale problems if commitments are missed. Third, skipping task breakdown leaves hidden dependencies that emerge mid-sprint and cause delays. The Scrum Master’s facilitation role is to ensure a healthy negotiation: they help the Product Owner and Development Team find a prioritized, realistic scope and prevent coercion or unrealistic promises. An example facilitation action is guiding a negotiation when the Product Owner insists on items that exceed capacity: surface the consequences, prioritize the highest-value subset, and document deferred items. Another facilitation step is reminding the team to reserve a small buffer for unplanned work. To test your judgment, imagine a team that reports only partial completion at sprint end; ask whether the root cause was capacity miscalculation, unclear acceptance criteria, or external interruptions, and choose a targeted remedy.

keyIdea.title: Avoiding mistakes
keyIdea.text: Facilitation by the Scrum Master and realistic planning prevent overcommitment and loss of team ownership.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Pitfalls & Scrum Master Role
Common mistakes
  • Overcommitment by ignoring current capacity adjustments.
  • Product Owner dictating scope; no negotiation.
  • Insufficient task breakdown that hides dependencies.
  • Zero buffer for unplanned work or bug fixes.
Remedy

Facilitate negotiation, adjust velocity for availability, require task breakdown, and reserve a small buffer.

Scrum Master actions
Facilitate a prioritization conversation when the Product Owner’s requests exceed capacity.
Encourage transparent estimates and highlight capacity adjustments.
Coach the team to break down stories and identify risky tasks early.
Assessment prompt
Multiple choice example
If the Product Owner insists on items beyond capacity, the Scrum Master should facilitate a negotiation to prioritize the most valuable subset and defer others.

narration.text: These three concepts are central when you plan a sprint. First, Sprint Planning is a time-boxed event where the Product Owner and Development Team agree on what will be done and how. It results in a Sprint Backlog and a Sprint Goal. Second, the Sprint Goal is a concise objective that describes the customer value to be delivered and allows the team to make trade-offs during the sprint. Third, capacity planning converts historical velocity into a practical selection by accounting for availability and a small buffer for unplanned work. Keep these concepts in mind when you participate in planning: they are the lenses that turn prioritized ideas into a realistic, team-owned plan. screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Short reminders to use during planning

narration.text: Use this quick reference while you run or participate in Sprint Planning. Remember to present high-priority backlog items with their value, negotiate selection against adjusted capacity, break selected stories into cross-functional tasks with owners and estimates, and finalize a single Sprint Goal that describes the value the sprint will deliver. Look out for the common warning signs: scope being dictated, capacity not adjusted, and missing task-level clarity. These short reminders help you maintain the ceremony’s purpose: predictable delivery of valuable increments through collaborative planning. Key Concepts — Quick Reference means present value, negotiate by capacity, decompose into tasks, and set a concise sprint goal.. In practical terms, short reminders to use during planning. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
